lines.text: Part 1. You will hear a woman phoning a swimming club because she wants to become a member. First, you have some time to look at questions 1 to 5.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 1 to 5.

lines.speaker: callum
lines.text: Hello, Westbrook Swimming Club, Callum speaking.

lines.speaker: ruth
lines.text: Oh, hi. I'm ringing about joining the club. I've just moved to the area, and I used to swim a lot, so I thought it was time to get back in the water.

lines.speaker: callum
lines.text: Great, you've come to the right place. I can take your details over the phone now, and then you'd just need to sign the form at your first session.

lines.speaker: ruth
lines.text: That would be perfect.

lines.speaker: callum
lines.text: Lovely. So can I start with your name?

lines.speaker: ruth
lines.text: Yes, it's Ruth Tennant.

lines.speaker: callum
lines.text: Ruth. And is that Tenant like someone who rents a flat? T-E-N-A-N-T?

lines.speaker: ruth
lines.text: Almost, but there are two Ns in the middle. So it's T-E-N-N-A-N-T. Tennant.

lines.speaker: callum
lines.text: Got it, sorry about that. And what's your address, Ruth?

lines.speaker: ruth
lines.text: I'm at 25 Mill Lane. Oh no, hang on, that's the number of the flat I've just left. I keep doing that. The new one is 52. So it's 52 Mill Lane.

lines.speaker: callum
lines.text: No problem. 52 Mill Lane. That's just past the bakery, isn't it?

lines.speaker: ruth
lines.text: That's right, the house with the blue door.

lines.speaker: callum
lines.text: Now, we put adult swimmers into three groups. Blue is for people still building their confidence, then there's silver, and gold is really for people who race in competitions. How would you describe your swimming?

lines.speaker: ruth
lines.text: Well, I swam for my school team, and I can still manage about a kilometre of front crawl without stopping. So I suppose gold might be right for me?

lines.speaker: callum
lines.text: Maybe eventually, but the gold group trains pretty hard. Since you've had a break, I'd suggest you start in silver, and the coach can move you up after a few weeks if you find it too easy.

lines.speaker: ruth
lines.text: Yes, that sounds sensible.

lines.speaker: callum
lines.text: Silver has two sessions a week, Monday and Wednesday, and most people come to one of them. Which would suit you better?

lines.speaker: ruth
lines.text: Monday would be ideal, really, because I work late on Wednesdays.

lines.speaker: callum
lines.text: Ah, I'm afraid Monday's completely full at the moment. There's a waiting list.

lines.speaker: ruth
lines.text: Oh, that's a shame. Well, I could probably swap my late shift. Let's say Wednesday, then.

lines.speaker: callum
lines.text: Brilliant. The Wednesday session is at the leisure centre pool on Station Road. The pool's open to the public until 8 o'clock, so our session starts at 8.15 and finishes at a quarter past nine.

lines.speaker: ruth
lines.text: That's quite late, but it's fine.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 6 to 10.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Now listen and answer questions 6 to 10.

lines.speaker: ruth
lines.text: Is there anything I need to bring with me? I've still got my old goggles somewhere, I think.

lines.speaker: callum
lines.text: Well, goggles are up to you, really. And every member gets a free club swimming cap, so don't buy one of those. But the coach does ask everyone in silver to bring their own fins, because she uses them a lot for leg training.

lines.speaker: ruth
lines.text: Fins? You mean flippers?

lines.speaker: callum
lines.text: Exactly, flippers. Short ones are best. We've got a few at the pool, but there are never enough to go round.

lines.speaker: ruth
lines.text: OK. And what about the cost? I saw something about a joining fee.

lines.speaker: callum
lines.text: Yes, there's a one-off joining fee, which covers your insurance and the club cap. It's usually 40 pounds, but if you join before the end of the month, it's only 20 pounds.

lines.speaker: ruth
lines.text: Oh, good timing, then. And then there's a monthly fee as well?

lines.speaker: callum
lines.text: That's right. It's 38 pounds a month, paid by direct debit. That includes your coaching and the pool hire. Now, the form also asks about any medical conditions the coach should know about. Is there anything like that?

lines.speaker: ruth
lines.text: Well, I had an operation on my knee a few years ago, but that's completely healed now. The only thing is that I have asthma. It's very mild, and I always keep my inhaler with me.

lines.speaker: callum
lines.text: OK, I'll put down asthma, then. Just leave your inhaler at the side of the pool where the coach can see it.

lines.speaker: ruth
lines.text: Will do. Oh, and is it easy to park at the leisure centre?

lines.speaker: callum
lines.text: Not really. The car park at the front gets very busy because of the gym. Some people use the supermarket car park across the road, but they've started giving fines to anyone who isn't shopping there. So the best thing is to use the free car park behind the church. It's only a two-minute walk. Right, last question. We like to know how people found out about us. Was it through a friend, or something else?

lines.speaker: ruth
lines.text: I think it was an advert in the local paper. No, actually, I'm wrong. I heard about you on the radio. There was an interview with one of your coaches on the breakfast show.

lines.speaker: callum
lines.text: Oh, that would have been Helen. I'll put down radio, then. Well, that's everything, Ruth. We'll see you next Wednesday.

lines.speaker: ruth
lines.text: Thanks so much, Callum. See you then.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: That is the end of Part 1. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

lines.text: Part 2. You will hear a librarian talking to a group of local residents about their refurbished community library. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 15.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 15.

lines.speaker: librarian
lines.text: Good evening, everyone, and thank you for coming. My name's Carla Novak, and I'm the manager here at Kingsmead Community Library. As you know, we've been closed for eight months while the building was refurbished, and we're finally ready to reopen on Saturday. So I wanted to tell you what's changed and what's stayed the same.

lines.speaker: librarian
lines.text: Let's start with the children's corner, which is still in the same place on the ground floor, just to the left of the main entrance. We did think about moving it upstairs, where there's more room, but parents told us very clearly that they didn't want to carry pushchairs up the stairs, so it's exactly the same size as before. What's different is the design. We held three workshops last spring with local families, and the children themselves drew the reading den and the little stage you'll see there.

lines.speaker: librarian
lines.text: Next to that, where the old magazine section used to be, are our four new study rooms. These are quiet rooms with a table, six chairs and a large screen, ideal for revising together or holding a meeting. A lot of libraries charge for rooms like these, but ours are completely free. The one thing to remember is that they're very popular, so you'll need to reserve one online, up to a week ahead.

lines.speaker: librarian
lines.text: Now, the local history room. For years it was squeezed into the basement, and the damp down there wasn't doing the old maps any good. So it's now on the top floor, in what used to be the staff office, and it has proper climate control. Many people think you need an appointment to look at the collection, but that's not the case. You can just walk in any time the library's open.

lines.speaker: librarian
lines.text: Something many of you asked for in our survey was a café, and I'm happy to say we now have one, run by a local charity that trains young people in catering. The library itself opens at nine, but the café opens its doors at eight every weekday, so you can grab a coffee on your way to work. It closes when we do, at six.

lines.speaker: librarian
lines.text: And finally, the digital lab on the first floor. It'll have computers with design software, a laser cutter and two 3D printers. When we first planned it, the idea was to keep it just for teenagers, but we've decided it should be open to all ages. Unfortunately, the printers have been held up by the supplier, and the room still needs its electrics checking, so the lab won't actually be ready until the spring.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 16 to 20.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Now listen and answer questions 16 to 20.

lines.speaker: librarian
lines.text: Now, a few practical changes. First, opening hours. In the survey, the most common request was for later opening on weekday evenings, but the budget simply wouldn't stretch to the extra staff. We also looked at opening earlier on Saturdays, but hardly anyone said they'd come in before ten. What we have managed to do is open on Sundays for the first time, from one until five in the afternoon. Weekday and Saturday hours stay exactly as they were.

lines.speaker: librarian
lines.text: You'll also notice the self-service machines by the entrance. They work just like the old ones for borrowing and returning, and the limit is still twelve items per card, so nothing's changed there. The new thing is that they can now take payments, so if you've used the printer or the photocopier, you can pay for it at the machine with a card instead of queuing at the desk. And the machines aren't there to replace staff: there will always be someone at the desk.

lines.speaker: librarian
lines.text: Joining the library has also become easier. Until now you had to come in person and fill in a paper form, but you can now join online through our website, and your card will be ready to collect the next time you visit. Children under twelve still need a parent or carer to sign for them, I'm afraid; that rule hasn't changed. And a question I get asked every week: no, your card won't work in other libraries in the county yet.

lines.speaker: librarian
lines.text: Now, Saturday's reopening. We'd originally planned for the day to begin with a talk by Grace Allardyce, the crime writer, but her train doesn't get in until eleven, so she'll be speaking just before lunch instead. So at ten o'clock, the doors will open with the choir from Hill Street Primary School singing on the front steps, and after that there'll be guided tours of the building every hour through the afternoon.

lines.speaker: librarian
lines.text: Last of all, how you can help. Lots of you have offered to donate books, which is kind, but our shelves are full, so please keep them for the summer book sale. The Friends of Kingsmead group is also doing well; they've got more members now than at any time in the last ten years. What we're really short of is volunteers for the after-school homework club, which starts again next month. If you could spare one afternoon a week, please put your name on the list by the door. Thank you, and see you on Saturday.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: That is the end of Part 2. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

lines.text: Part 4. You will hear a lecture about the history of lighthouses. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.

lines.speaker: lecturer
lines.text: Good morning, everyone. Today, in our series on maritime history, I'm going to look at lighthouses: how the technology behind them changed, and how sailors learned to tell one light from another.

lines.speaker: lecturer
lines.text: The most famous lighthouse of the ancient world was, of course, the Pharos of Alexandria, built in Egypt in the third century BC. Ancient accounts suggest it was well over a hundred metres tall, with a fire burning at the top. Remarkably, it stood for something like fifteen hundred years. It's often assumed that it was destroyed in a war, or by invaders, but in fact the historical records point clearly to a series of earthquakes, which damaged it again and again until the last parts collapsed in the fourteenth century.

lines.speaker: lecturer
lines.text: After the Roman period, very few new lighthouses were built in Europe for centuries. Where coastal lights did exist in the medieval period, they were usually looked after not by governments or by merchants but by monks, who saw keeping a light burning for sailors as a religious duty.

lines.speaker: lecturer
lines.text: By the seventeenth century, though, lighthouses had become a business. In England, for example, private individuals could obtain the right to build a lighthouse, and they made their money by collecting a toll from every ship that passed it or came into a nearby port. People sometimes describe this as a tax, but that's misleading, because none of the money went to the state. Some owners became extremely rich, and shipowners complained about the quality of the lights they were paying for.

lines.speaker: lecturer
lines.text: And they had a point. Most early lighthouses burned coal in an open iron basket at the top of the tower. On a calm night this worked quite well, but in wind and rain the fire would die down, and the keeper had to spend hours working a pair of bellows to keep it bright enough to be seen. It was exhausting work, and a single coal light could use several hundred tonnes of fuel a year.

lines.speaker: lecturer
lines.text: Enclosing the light behind glass solved the problem of the wind, so towers began to use candles, and later oil lamps, inside a glass room called the lantern. But this created a new difficulty. The lamps produced a great deal of smoke, and soot built up on the inside of the glass so quickly that half the light could be hidden within a few hours.

lines.speaker: lecturer
lines.text: The real breakthrough came in the 1820s, from the French physicist Augustin Fresnel. Until then, the best lighthouses used large curved mirrors behind the lamp to direct the light out to sea. These mirrors were heavy, and they wasted a lot of the light. Fresnel replaced them with a lens made of rings of glass prisms, arranged around the lamp a bit like a beehive, which bent almost all of the light into a single powerful beam. A light that had been visible for a few miles could now be seen from more than twenty miles away.

lines.speaker: lecturer
lines.text: Now, as the number of lighthouses grew, a new problem appeared. If a sailor could see a light, how did he know which lighthouse it was? Mistaking one for another could be just as dangerous as having no light at all.

lines.speaker: lecturer
lines.text: During the day, the answer was the tower itself. Many lighthouses were painted with stripes, either horizontal bands or spirals, in black and white or red and white, so that each one had its own distinctive appearance from the sea. These patterns are known as daymarks, and many of them are still in use today.

lines.speaker: lecturer
lines.text: At night, of course, the paint is no help, so each light was given what's called a characteristic: a particular pattern of flashes and dark periods. One light might flash twice every ten seconds, another once every five. To produce these flashes, the lens had to turn smoothly at a precise speed. The solution, from the 1890s onwards, was to float the whole lens on a bath of mercury, which allowed a lens weighing several tonnes to be turned by a simple clockwork mechanism. The disadvantage, as we now know, is that mercury is highly toxic, and many keepers suffered from its effects.

lines.speaker: lecturer
lines.text: The third method was for fog, when neither the tower nor the light could be seen. The earliest fog signals were bells, and at some stations cannons were fired at regular intervals. By the late nineteenth century, these had largely been replaced by sirens, powered by compressed air, which could be heard several miles away. Even so, sound behaves unpredictably over water, and sailors were warned never to rely on a fog signal alone.

lines.speaker: lecturer
lines.text: Finally, in the twentieth century, lighthouses began to send out radio signals. From the 1920s, radio beacons allowed ships with the right equipment to identify a station, and even work out its direction, in thick fog and from far beyond the range of any light. Each beacon transmitted its own identity in Morse code, a short sequence of dots and dashes repeated over and over.

lines.speaker: lecturer
lines.text: Today, of course, most ships rely on satellite navigation, and almost every lighthouse in the world is automatic. Next week, we'll look at the lives of the keepers themselves.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: That is the end of Part 4. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For most of human history, the idea that other stars might have planets of their own was a matter for philosophers rather than astronomers. Today it is a matter of routine measurement. More than five thousand planets orbiting other stars, known as exoplanets, have now been confirmed, and new candidates are announced almost every week. Yet very few of these worlds have ever been seen directly. A planet shines only by reflecting the light of its star, and from many light years away it is lost in that star's glare, rather like a firefly circling a powerful searchlight. Instead, astronomers have learnt to detect planets by the effects they have on the stars they orbit.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The first successful technique relied on the fact that a planet does not simply circle a stationary star. Both bodies actually orbit a shared centre of mass, so as the planet travels around, the star makes a small, regular movement of its own, drifting slightly towards the Earth and then away again. This wobble cannot be seen in photographs, but it can be detected in the star's light, which appears very slightly bluer as the star approaches and redder as it moves away. In 1995 this method revealed the first planet known to orbit an ordinary Sun-like star: a giant world, about half the mass of Jupiter, that completes an orbit in just over four days. Its discovery surprised many astronomers, who had not expected such a large planet to exist so close to its star.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The method that has since produced the largest number of discoveries works in a different way. If a planet's orbit happens to be lined up so that, seen from the Earth, it passes directly in front of its star, it blocks a tiny fraction of the star's light. This event is called a transit. A planet the size of Jupiter crossing a star like the Sun reduces its brightness by about one per cent; an Earth-sized planet, by less than one hundredth of one per cent. Because only a small proportion of planetary orbits are aligned in this way, astronomers cannot study stars one at a time. They need to watch huge numbers simultaneously. The Kepler space telescope, launched in 2009, monitored roughly 150,000 stars in a single patch of sky, measuring the brightness of each one every half an hour for four years.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: According to Dr Ingrid Solberg of the Halvard Observatory, who has spent fifteen years analysing data of this kind, the work begins with a graph. For every star, the measurements of brightness are plotted against time to produce what is called a light curve. Computer programs then search each light curve for a shallow dip, the sign that something may have crossed the face of the star. A single dip, Solberg warns, proves very little, since dark spots on the star's surface or a brief fault in the instrument can produce a similar effect. The team therefore waits until it has recorded at least three dips of the same depth, separated by equal intervals. The time between them gives the planet's orbital period, while the depth of each dip reveals how large the planet is compared with its star.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Even a regular signal may be misleading. The most common source of confusion is a so-called eclipsing binary: a pair of stars that orbit each other and take turns to pass in front of one another. If such a pair lies far behind the target star, its faint light can blend with the target's, creating dips that look remarkably like those of a planet. In one survey, Solberg's group found that roughly one candidate in five had to be rejected for this reason. Astronomers therefore look carefully at the shape of each dip, since a star partly hidden by another star tends to produce a V-shaped curve, while a planet usually produces a flatter, U-shaped one. They also compare alternate dips: if every second dip is deeper than the others, two stars of different brightness are probably responsible.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: A candidate that survives these tests is not yet a confirmed planet. The next step is to turn a large ground-based telescope towards the star and, using an instrument called a spectrograph, look for the wobble described earlier. This combination of methods is especially powerful. The transit reveals the planet's diameter, while the wobble reveals its mass, and from these two figures astronomers can calculate its density. Dr Kwame Asante of Northmoor University, who leads a follow-up programme, describes density as 'the first real clue to what a world is made of'. A dense planet is likely to be rocky, like the Earth, whereas one with a low density is probably composed largely of gas.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Transits offer one further opportunity. As a planet crosses its star, a little starlight passes through the planet's atmosphere on its way to us, and the gases there absorb particular colours. By comparing the light during and outside a transit, astronomers have detected water vapour, carbon dioxide and other substances in the atmospheres of distant worlds. The technique has limitations, however. Large planets in tight orbits are the easiest to find, so current catalogues contain far more of them than the galaxy probably does. A planet resembling the Earth, orbiting a star like the Sun once a year, produces only one faint dip every twelve months, and confirming it requires several years of patient observation.

passage.title: The return of the hand loom

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: On a weekday morning in Kelderby, a small market town in the north of England, the clatter of wooden looms can be heard from a converted chapel on the high street. Inside, eleven weavers are at work, and a notice by the door explains that the waiting list for apprenticeships is now closed for the year. Thirty years ago this scene would have seemed impossible. Kelderby cloth, a dense woollen fabric once worn by farmers and shepherds across the region, was widely regarded as a dead craft, of interest only to museums. Its return raises questions not only about how traditional skills are rescued, but about what exactly is being rescued, and for whom.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The cloth has a long history. From the early eighteenth century it was woven by families in their own cottages, using wool from local sheep, and sold to merchants who visited the town on market days. At the height of the trade, in the 1850s, there were said to be around two thousand hand looms in Kelderby and the surrounding villages. The arrival of power looms in large mills, which could produce cloth far more cheaply, brought a long decline. By 1900 only a few hundred hand-weavers remained, and after the Second World War their number fell to a handful. In 1987 the last of them, Walter Penrose, closed his workshop, and his looms were stored in a neighbour's barn.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The revival began almost by accident. In 1994 Elspeth Rowan, a textile designer from Glasgow, bought Penrose's looms at an auction, intending to use them for her own experimental work. She soon became fascinated by the cloth itself. Penrose, then in his eighties, agreed to teach her, but much of what she needed to know was contained in a set of family pattern books written in a private notation that even he could only partly read. Rowan spent two winters decoding it with the help of a retired engineer before she could reproduce the traditional designs. From the start, she insisted that the cloth should not become a museum piece. 'A craft survives only if people want to wear what it makes,' she says. 'Otherwise you are just preserving a performance.'

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Not everyone accepts that what Kelderby produces today is the same cloth. Dr Anil Mehta, a textile historian at Northgate University, points out that most of the revived fabric is woven from soft merino wool imported from abroad, and coloured with synthetic dyes in shades that would have astonished Penrose's grandparents. The original cloth, by contrast, was made from coarse local fleece and dyed with plants such as heather and lichen. Yet Mehta does not regard this as a failure. Traditions, he argues, have always changed to suit new markets, and the weavers of the 1850s were themselves quick to copy fashionable patterns from elsewhere. In his view, a revival is always partly an invention, and there is nothing dishonest about that.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The economics of the craft remain difficult. A length of cloth large enough for a single jacket takes an experienced weaver about three days to make, and as a result hand-woven Kelderby cloth costs roughly ten times as much as a similar fabric from a modern mill. Hannah Kowalczyk, who advises a regional crafts council, describes the market as small but loyal. Buyers, she says, are paying for the story and for the maker's name as much as for the cloth itself. Since online sales began in 2011, demand has grown steadily, but Kowalczyk sees a danger in this. Weavers cannot easily increase their output, and some have been tempted to use partly mechanised looms, a practice she believes could damage the reputation that the revival has built.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Learning the craft properly takes time. Rowan estimates that an apprentice needs around five years to become fully skilled, and the workshop accepts only two new trainees each year. Most are in their twenties, and a surprising number have left office jobs to take up the loom. The sociologist Dr Grace Okafor, who interviewed forty craft workers in northern England for a recent study, found that few of them were motivated mainly by money. What they valued most was control over how they spent their working day and the satisfaction of producing a finished object. However, Okafor also found that more than half depended on a partner's income or a second job, which suggests that the revival rests on a fragile base.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The cloth's recent fame has brought its own tensions. In 2016 the Swedish fashion designer Tobias Lindqvist used Kelderby cloth in a collection shown in Paris, arguing that hand-made fabric gives clothing an authenticity that factories cannot imitate. Orders increased sharply. Some residents, however, felt that the cloth their grandparents had worn for work was being turned into a luxury that they could no longer afford. Rowan takes these concerns seriously. The question, she suggests, is no longer whether the craft will survive, but who it will survive for.

passage.title: The four-day week: a result, not a remedy

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Few ideas about work have travelled so quickly from the margins to the mainstream as the four-day week. A decade ago it was the preserve of a handful of campaigning groups and unusually idealistic employers; today it is debated in parliaments, tested by large companies and promised in election manifestos. The appeal is obvious. The five-day week, itself the outcome of long campaigns in the early twentieth century, has remained essentially unchanged for generations, while the technology with which we work has been transformed beyond recognition. Surely, the argument runs, the dividends of that transformation should be paid partly in time. I have some sympathy with this view. But the evidence offered in its support is thinner, and far more conditional, than its advocates tend to admit.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The case rests largely on a series of organised trials. The most widely cited, coordinated by the Corran Institute, involved 74 organisations, ranging from software developers to a fish-and-chip shop, which reduced working hours by a fifth for six months while keeping pay unchanged. The reported outcomes were remarkable. Sickness absence fell by around a third, staff described markedly lower levels of exhaustion, and revenues across the participating firms remained broadly stable. Perhaps most tellingly, nine in ten of the organisations chose to continue with the shorter week once the trial had ended. For many commentators, the matter was settled.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: It should not have been. Every firm in the trial had volunteered, and organisations that volunteer for such an experiment are, almost by definition, those whose managers already believe it will succeed and whose work is most easily reorganised. Much of the evidence, moreover, came from surveys in which employees reported their own well-being and productivity, knowing that a favourable verdict would help to secure the extra day off. Even the revenue figures are difficult to interpret over a period as short as six months, during which the novelty of the arrangement may itself have lifted morale and effort. None of this proves that the results were wrong. It means only that they tell us what happened in an enthusiastic and self-selected group, not what would happen if the policy were adopted widely.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A more useful question is where the gains came from, when they did occur. Dr Leonie Marchetti of the Valemont School of Management, who has studied the trial firms in detail, finds a striking pattern. Organisations that used the change as an opportunity to redesign work – cancelling routine meetings, protecting periods of uninterrupted concentration and abandoning tasks that no longer served any purpose – generally maintained their output. Those that simply compressed forty hours into four longer days fared much worse, reporting fatigue, mistakes and, eventually, a quiet return to the old pattern. The lesson, as I read it, is that the extra day is not in itself the source of any benefit. It is the reward for eliminating waste, and where there is little waste to eliminate, there is little to reward.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: That distinction matters enormously, because a large part of the economy does not work in the way that offices do. In a hospital ward, a classroom or a care home, the service consists largely of being present: a nurse who works fewer hours is not a nurse who finishes the same work faster, but one who is absent for a day that someone else must cover. When the city of Strandvik shortened shifts in two of its residential homes for the elderly, staff reported better health and lower turnover, but the authority had to recruit fourteen additional carers to maintain the same level of care, and the experiment was abandoned after two years on grounds of cost. The improvement was real; so was the bill.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: There is a further risk, which advocates rarely address. If the four-day week spreads chiefly among professionals whose output is hard to observe and easy to compress, while nurses, drivers and shop assistants continue to work five days or more, the result will be a new and highly visible division in the labour market. Leisure time, already unequally distributed, would become still more so, and the gain would go to precisely those workers who are already the best paid. Surveys suggest that many employees would in any case prefer greater flexibility over when they work to a fixed reduction in the number of days, but this preference receives far less attention than the more eye-catching proposal.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of this means that the four-day week should be dismissed. Where it emerges from a genuine reorganisation of work, it appears to benefit both employees and employers, and firms should be free to pursue it. What I doubt is the wisdom of treating it as a target, still less of imposing it by law, as some politicians now propose. A legal requirement would push hospitals and schools towards the costly arithmetic of Strandvik, while doing little for productivity in offices where the necessary reorganisation has not taken place. A better course would be for governments to invest in measuring output more accurately, particularly in services, so that firms can see where time is being wasted. Shorter weeks may well follow. They should be the result of working better, not a substitute for it.
